content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain how the Haber process produces ammonia
Explain the conditions chosen for the Haber process
Describe the Contact process for sulfuric acid
Explain compromises between rate and yield in industry
Industrial chemists must balance many factors when running reactions at scale. For reversible reactions, they must consider both
(how much product). Often, conditions that favour one don't favour the other.
Hydrogen: from natural gas + steam, or electrolysis of water
Left side: 4 moles of gas (1 N₂ + 3 H₂)
Right side: 2 moles of gas (2 NH₃)
High pressure favours fewer moles → shifts RIGHT
Low temperature favours exothermic direction → more NH₃
Would take too long to reach equilibrium
Not so high that yield is too low
Does NOT change position of equilibrium
Allows lower temperature to be used while maintaining reasonable rate

N₂ and H₂ enter reactor (1:3 ratio)
Pass over iron catalyst at 450°C, 200 atm
Recycling eventually converts most of the gases
Lower temperature would give better yield
But reaction would be too slow
Even at low pressure, yield is high (99%)
High pressure equipment not worth the cost
Use catalysts to speed up at lower temperatures
Explain why the Haber process uses high pressure.
There are 4 moles of gas on the left (1 + 3)
There are 2 moles of gas on the right
High pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer gas moles
This means equilibrium shifts to the RIGHT
Explain why a low temperature would give the highest yield in the Haber process, but is not used industrially.
The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = -92 kJ/mol)
Low temperature favours the exothermic direction (forward)
This would shift equilibrium to the right → more ammonia
However, at low temperatures the rate of reaction is very slow
It would take too long to reach equilibrium
A compromise temperature of 450°C is used
This gives a reasonable rate AND a reasonable yield
Explain the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process.
The iron catalyst speeds up the reaction
It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
This allows a lower temperature to be used while maintaining a reasonable rate
However, the catalyst does NOT change the equilibrium position
It does NOT increase the yield
The same ratio of products to reactants is formed, just faster
Catalysts only speed up reaching equilibrium; they don't change position
Thinking higher temperature always gives more product
For exothermic reactions, higher temperature decreases yield
Forgetting about recycling in industrial processes
Recycling unreacted gases allows high overall conversion
State the equation for the Haber process and the conditions used. (4 marks)
Explain why high pressure increases the yield of ammonia. (3 marks)
Explain why 450°C is described as a 'compromise' temperature in the Haber process. (4 marks)
The Contact process uses a temperature of 450°C even though lower temperatures would give a higher yield. Explain why. (3 marks)
In the Haber process, unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled. Explain why this is done. (3 marks)
Explain why the Contact process operates at atmospheric pressure despite having more moles of gas on the left of the equation. (3 marks)
Industrial process to make ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen
Industrial process to make sulfuric acid
A balance between two opposing factors
To return unreacted materials to the reactor
High pressure favours fewer moles (more NH₃)
Unreacted gases recycled for high overall conversion
High yield achieved without high pressure
